summary: Lists the requirements for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol when paths cross Autonomous System boundaries in MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering. It builds on the generic PCE requirements. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Planning a trip that crosses several countries needs a map-helper that can talk across borders. This memo lists what that helper protocol must be able to do between different networks.

questions: pce communication protocol across autonomous systems
how do pces cooperate across domains
subtitle: Requirements for computing network paths that cross administrative boundaries.

tldr.problem: When traffic-engineered paths must cross multiple Autonomous Systems (ASes) controlled by different operators, PCE path computation must handle hiding topology details, enforcing policies at boundaries, and selecting between multiple possible ASBRs.
tldr.mechanism: The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCECP) must support specifying sequences of ASes in a path, preserving confidentiality of intra-AS topology, rate-limiting policies, and protecting path computations across multiple domains.
tldr.outcome: Service providers can compute optimum TE paths across multiple networks without exposing internal topology or violating peering agreements.

today: RFC 5376 is informational, extending generic PCECP requirements to inter-AS scenarios. The PCECP itself was standardized in companion RFCs. PCE-based path computation remains relevant for traffic engineering across multiple domains, particularly in multi-provider environments, though deployment has focused on intra-domain and intra-provider scenarios.

sections.title: Why Inter-AS Path Computation Matters
sections.content:
In MPLS traffic engineering, Label Switched Paths (LSPs) can span multiple Autonomous Systems. A Service Provider might offer a backbone, while partner providers operate customer edge networks. For traffic-engineered services to work end-to-end, the system must compute paths optimally across these administrative boundaries.

A Path Computation Element (PCE) is a network component that computes constrained paths. The PCE Communication Protocol (PCECP) is how clients and other PCEs request path computations. This RFC extends basic PCECP requirements to the inter-AS case, where paths cross between networks operated by different organizations.

Traditional signaling protocols like RSVP-TE compute paths hop-by-hop as they signal across the network. This works within a domain but becomes inefficient across multiple domains. PCEs pre-compute optimum paths, separating computation from the signaling itself, and can optimize globally across domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you set up a data path across multiple networks run by different companies, you need to ask 'Is there a good route?' but without revealing each company's network secrets or violating business agreements.

sections.title: PCE Architecture for Inter-AS Paths
sections.content:
In inter-AS deployment, there are two types of PCE. An Intra-AS PCE computes paths within a single AS. An Inter-AS PCE (at the network boundary) cooperates with intra-AS PCEs and other inter-AS PCEs to compute end-to-end paths.

A typical scenario: a client in AS1 asks its Inter-AS PCE1 to compute a path to a destination in AS3. PCE1 determines the route passes through AS2 and asks PCE2 (AS2's Inter-AS PCE). PCE2 asks its intra-AS PCE to find a path within AS2 that enters at ASBR3 and exits at ASBR7. The intra-AS PCE responds with that segment. PCE2 then asks PCE3 (AS3's Inter-AS PCE) to compute the segment from ASBR7 to the destination. Each PCE returns its segment, and PCE2 assembles them into the full path and returns it to PCE1, which returns it to the client.

This cooperative model requires PCECP to carry AS-level information while respecting domain boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Each company has its own path expert (intra-AS PCE) and a boundary expert (inter-AS PCE). They call each other, asking for path segments without revealing their internal networks, then stitch the pieces together.

sections.title: PCECP Requirements for Inter-AS
sections.content:
AS and ASBR specification: A path computation request must be able to specify a preferred sequence of ASes or specific Autonomous System Border Routers (ASBRs) to traverse. For example, 'compute a path via ASBR1 (mandatory) or ASBR2 (optional).' This allows operators to enforce policies like preferring specific peers.

Exclusions: Requests must support excluding certain ASes or ASBRs from the computed path, for example to avoid congested or untrusted paths.

Sender identification: When an inter-AS PCE requests computation from another inter-AS PCE, it must identify itself and its AS so that local policy rules can be applied. A PCE in AS2 might trust requests from AS1's PCE but reject requests from AS4.

Protection: Requests must specify whether protection (1:1 detours or facility backup) is needed, and whether it is required across all ASes or just specific ones.

Disjoint paths: Requests for multiple disjoint paths must support AS-diversity—for example, 'give me two paths that do not share ASes,' allowing operators to guard against AS-level failures.

Response handling: A response must be able to convey path segments with identifiers instead of full explicit hops, preserving topology confidentiality. For instance, an inter-AS PCE returns a segment identifier that signals (e.g., RSVP-TE) will expand during path setup.

Cost reporting: Responses must carry cumulative path cost across ASes, allowing the requesting PCE to compare options.
sections.plainLanguage: Requests must say which ASBRs you prefer or must avoid, who is asking, and whether you need backups. Responses should hide internal details but reveal the total cost.

sections.title: Security and Policy in Inter-AS PCECP
sections.content:
Key management: PCEs that peer across AS boundaries must authenticate each other and protect their communications. Manual configuration works for established peering relationships; automated key discovery is needed when PCE-to-PCE relationships are dynamic.

Policy enforcement: Each PCE applies local policy to requests it receives, rewriting parameters (like priority or differentiated services class) or rejecting non-compliant requests. The PCECP must support error messages when a request violates local policy.

Confidentiality: Each AS should hide its internal topology from other ASes. PCECP responses should carry segment identifiers, not explicit hop-by-hop paths. Additionally, a PCE should be able to mask its identity so that other ASes cannot infer its role in a computation chain.

Information falsification: When multiple PCEs cooperate, downstream PCEs might falsify path segments computed by upstream PCEs. For example, PCE2 might modify the segment PCE3 returned. PCECP must allow PCEs to verify that the signaled path matches what was computed, and protocols (like signaling) must echo back computed segment identifiers.

Operational scope: Scaling is limited: typically only a few dozen PCEs per AS and a few peering relationships, so the n-squared growth in possible PCE-to-PCE relationships is manageable.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEs must trust each other, enforce rules at boundaries, hide secrets, and prevent tampering. Each AS trusts only its own PCE initially.

sections.title: Management and Monitoring
sections.content:
PCE systems must support standard management: MIB modules for configuration, statistics, and alarms. In the inter-AS case, MIBs must allow configuration per-AS, not just per-peer. For example, an operator might set different keep-alive frequencies for different neighboring ASes.

Diagnostic tools must enable failure detection and status checking across AS boundaries. Statistics should be analyzable per-neighbor-AS so operators can see which AS relationships are healthy.

Trap (alert) functions must trigger when thresholds are crossed, and these thresholds should be specifiable per-AS and per-PCE peer. For instance, 'alert if we lose connectivity to AS2's PCE' or 'warn if AS2 responds slowly'.

Basic liveliness detection is specified in generic PCECP requirements; inter-AS deployment should allow per-peer control of keep-alive frequency and dead intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need dashboards and alerts for each AS relationship to spot problems quickly.
